title: 2 Kings 16:10–20
context: Ahaz travels to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser, sees an altar there, and sends its design to Urijah the priest, who builds a copy. Ahaz offers on the new altar, moves the bronze altar of the LORD aside, and orders the regular sacrifices to be made on the new one. He also strips the temple furnishings, removing the basin stands and the sea from the bronze oxen, and alters the temple entrances because of the king of Assyria. Second Chronicles 28 adds that he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus and shut the temple doors.

verses.text: King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath Pileser king of Assyria, and saw the altar that was at Damascus; and King Ahaz sent to Urijah the priest a drawing of the altar and plans to build it.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz goes to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser and sends Urijah a design of the altar there. Arminian readers see a king choosing to bring foreign worship patterns into the LORD's house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God had given the pattern for his altar (Exodus 27). Ahaz replaces God's design with a model copied from a pagan city.

verses.text: Urijah the priest built an altar. According to all that King Ahaz had sent from Damascus, so Urijah the priest made it for the coming of King Ahaz from Damascus.
verses.arminianNotes: Urijah the priest builds the altar according to Ahaz's plans. Arminian readers note that the priest freely cooperates, showing how religious leaders can be complicit in a king's unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Urijah follows the king's command without recorded protest. The narrator lets the priest's compliance speak for itself.

verses.text: When the king had come from Damascus, the king saw the altar; and the king came near to the altar, and offered on it.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz returns, approaches the altar, and offers on it. Arminian readers note that the king takes a leading role in worship at the new altar, giving it his full endorsement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ahaz acts as the chief worshiper at the altar he commissioned. The king's personal participation marks this as a deliberate change in Judah's worship.

verses.text: He burned his burnt offering and his meal offering, poured his drink offering, and sprinkled the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.
verses.arminianNotes: He offers burnt, meal, drink, and peace offerings on the altar. Arminian readers note that he uses the familiar offerings of Israel's law, giving foreign worship the appearance of continuity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the forms of Israel's offerings are kept but placed on a foreign altar. Outward correctness cannot sanctify worship that disregards God's command.

verses.text: The bronze altar, which was before the LORD, he brought from the front of the house, from between his altar and the LORD’s house, and put it on the north side of his altar.
verses.arminianNotes: He moves the bronze altar from its place before the LORD to the north side of the new altar. Arminian readers see the LORD's altar literally pushed aside, a picture of God displaced from the center of Judah's worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the altar "which was before the LORD" is relocated to make room for the king's altar. The physical change reflects a spiritual one.

verses.text: King Ahaz commanded Urijah the priest, saying, “On the great altar burn the morning burnt offering, the evening meal offering, the king’s burnt offering and his meal offering, with the burnt offering of all the people of the land, their meal offering, and their drink offerings; and sprinkle on it all the blood of the burnt offering, and all the blood of the sacrifice; but the bronze altar will be for me to inquire by.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz commands the regular sacrifices on the great altar, keeping the bronze altar "for me to inquire by." Arminian readers note that he reorders the temple worship to suit his preferences, retaining the old altar only for his own use.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the king assumes authority over worship that belonged to God's word. The text does not explain what inquiring by the bronze altar meant, and interpreters differ.

verses.text: Urijah the priest did so, according to all that King Ahaz commanded.
verses.arminianNotes: Urijah does all that Ahaz commands. Arminian readers note again the priest's compliance, which helps the king's changes take root in Judah's worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repeated statement of Urijah's obedience to the king. The priesthood that should have guarded God's worship instead carries out the king's innovations.

verses.text: King Ahaz cut off the panels of the bases, and removed the basin from off them, and took down the sea from off the bronze oxen that were under it, and put it on a pavement of stone.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz cuts off the panels of the bases, removes the basin, and takes the sea from the bronze oxen. Arminian readers see him dismantling the temple furnishings Solomon made (1 Kings 7:25).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the stripping may have supplied metal for tribute, though the text does not say. Either way, the glory of Solomon's temple is diminished under Ahaz.

verses.text: He removed the covered way for the Sabbath that they had built in the house, and the king’s outer entrance to the LORD’s house, because of the king of Assyria.
verses.arminianNotes: He removes the covered way for the Sabbath and the king's outer entrance "because of the king of Assyria." Arminian readers note that the reason given shows how deeply Assyria's influence shaped Ahaz's decisions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the precise nature of these changes is unclear. The narrator's point is that the king of Assyria, not the LORD, now governs what happens in the LORD's house.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Ahaz which he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Ahaz's acts are in the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Arminian readers note that 2 Chronicles 28:22 adds that "in the time of his distress, he trespassed yet more against the LORD."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Chronicles 28:23 records his sacrificing to "the gods of Damascus," and that "they were the ruin of him and of all Israel."

verses.text: Ahaz slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in David’s city; and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz is buried in David's city, and Hezekiah succeeds him. Arminian readers note the hope in this transition, since Hezekiah will lead one of Judah's great reforms.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God preserves David's line even through Ahaz. From the son of one of Judah's most unfaithful kings comes one of its most faithful.
